script: A lawyer's pro revenge on a landlord. The landlord's driving me nuts," he said, pulling me aside in the cramped kitchen of The Vault. The smell of oregano and old steel lingered in the air, like a bad ex you can't shake. I was on my lunch break, trying to enjoy a sandwich between a stack of old safe deposit boxes that looked more like relics than a dining room. I stared at him, half‑laughing, half‑suspicious. "The landlord drives everyone nuts," I shot back, because if he had a problem, it was about to be solved. I was a subtenant, sharing the space with a grizzled lawyer named Aaron, and the landlord was a walking nightmare. He'd been changing locks, threatening, demanding extra rent for snow removal, parking lot repairs, and whatever else he could find. If you were late on rent, the lock changed. If you tried to fight, the lock changed. It was simple, brutal, and the building felt like a hostage situation. The Vault's owner was a small‑time entrepreneur who'd turned the basement into a restaurant, but the landlord still had a grip on the property. He'd given the owner a letter earlier that day, a list of ridiculous expenses that spanned years. The landlord was always trying to squeeze more from us, and the lease said he could change locks if we didn't pay. I read the letter, and my stomach dropped. I had a feeling the landlord was trying to squeeze every ounce of cash out of the restaurant before it left town. The letter was a threat wrapped in a demand. I had to act, or we'd all end up locked out for no reason. (I know, right?) I asked the owner if we could make the landlord hate us, because if we didn't, the landlord would keep doing this. "He knows I am moving the restaurant," the owner replied, "I think he's trying to grab as much money as possible before I go." The landlord had a grudge against the vault. He wouldn't let us take it with us, even though it weighed a hundred tons. The lease required us to remove it and restore the space, which would cost a fortune. The landlord threatened to sue if we left it. The owner was terrified, but I was not. "Send your lease to my office," I said, "and I'll look it over." The lease was a tangled mess, a renewal of a renewal of a lease that dated back to the post‑WWII era when a bank first leased the building and installed the vault. The restaurant had signed a lease that left the landlord liable for the vault. If the restaurant defaulted, the landlord could sue a shell company. The landlord had a guarantee clause that made the restaurant owner personally liable. The cost to remove and restore the vault would bankrupt the owner. The stakes were high: if we failed, the landlord would keep us locked out and the restaurant would die. I sat in my office, the lease spread out like a crime scene. The guarantee clause was the last thing I wanted to see. The landlord's threats were a ticking time bomb. I thought about how the landlord had been changing locks on anyone who tried to leave, and I imagined the worst. I knew that if we didn't act now, the landlord would lock us out, we'd lose the lease, the restaurant would close, and the landlord would be left with a property that was essentially a dead zone. The stakes were my client's future. I had to find a way to fight back. (I know, right?) But here's the thing: I was a lawyer, not a landlord. I had no resources, no big law firm to back me. I had to be clever. I called the restaurant owner, and we talked for hours about the lease and the landlord's demands. He was scared, but I told him I could save him, for a price. He sent me a check for five thousand dollars and another for the agent. I needed a real estate agent who knew the ins and outs of commercial leases. I went to Aaron's office, and he was like, "You buying a house?" I said, "Nope." Aaron gave me the number of a guy he knew from the old school days, a real estate agent who had a reputation for being ruthless. I met the agent, we shook hands, and I paid him a fee. The agent had a plan, but it was risky. (I know, right?) The next day I was back at The Vault for lunch, because I needed to talk to the owner again. He greeted me like a villain and told me the landlord was there. The landlord was a big, beefy man who ate a rack of lamb with his hands like a man who thinks he's a king. He was in the corner, surrounded by other tenants. The owner and I sat in the vault room, the door almost closed, and we ate carbonara while I slid a demand letter across the table. "We're demanding that the landlord release all the restaurant equipment," I said, "the ovens, the freezers, the ventilation. We're also demanding that the bank vault be released within seven business days." The owner looked at me, stunned. The landlord laughed at us. "I can do what I want," he said, wiping his greasy hands on a napkin. I told him I needed that in writing, because my client might sue. He said, "Sue all you like." He gave me a formal response by the end of the day. I took the letter down and showed it to my client. The client was like, "How did you do that?" I said, "Trade secret." (I know, right?) The following month the restaurant moved out. The building was empty, the vault still in place. The landlord was furious. He claimed the lease had fallen through, the bank had backed out, and he'd lost his chance to make money. He came to my office a few days later, a wild look in his eyes. He said, "I know you were behind this." He accused me of using the agent to trick him into keeping the vault. He threatened to sue the restaurant, the agent, and me. I told him I would fight back. He left, but I didn't let him. I kept my head down, my mind on the next move. (I know, right?) The landlord didn't sue. He had no contract to sue on. He had only a vague letter of intent, a non‑binding offer. The landlord had no leverage. The lease was still on the table, and the landlord's threat was just a threat. The restaurant was gone, the vault remained, and I had a client who was ready to move on. The landlord's power was slipping. The next step was to keep the landlord at bay. The stakes were still high: if the landlord got the vault, he could use it to make a profit. If he didn't, my client could move on. I had to keep my client safe, and I had to keep my job. (I know, right?)
